title: Lalitaditya Builds the City That Laughed

title_i18n.en: Lalitaditya Builds the City That Laughed

subtitle: When the Karkota king carved a laughing capital from the Kashmiri plain
era: Parihasapura and Karkota urban building, c. 740s-760 CE
region: Parihasapura near modern Paraspore, northwest of Srinagar
moral: A city can announce what a kingdom believes about itself.

sources.citation: Kalhana, Rajatarangini, Book IV, vv. 194-204; Stein trans., Vol. 1 (1900), pp. 162-167
sources.note: Detailed literary description of Parihasapura's royal and religious buildings.

sources.citation: M.A. Stein, site notes and plan of Parihasapura in Kalhana's Rajatarangini, Vol. 2, Appendix A (1900)
sources.note: Surface survey matching ruins at Paraspore/Kani Shahar to Kalhana's account.

sources.citation: Hermann Goetz, Studies in the History and Art of Kashmir and the Indian Himalaya (1969), pp. 11-16
sources.note: Art-historical discussion of the complex and its possible wider influences.

panels.shot: sweeping wide shot over misty Kashmir plain with faint ruins, ghosted vision of a radiant ancient city rising above

dialogue.text: In the age of the Karkotas, Lalitaditya built Parihasapura, the City of Laughter—palace, Vishnu shrines and a giant copper Buddha together—yet today almost nothing stands. How does a capital vanish, and a vision still endure?

panels.shot: epic aerial over the Kashmir valley, river Jhelum snaking through fields toward low hills

dialogue.text: Northwest of Srinagar, above the Jhelum, the plain lies quiet. But Kalhana’s chronicle says this ground once held a planned royal city, laid out by a king who thought in stone and sunlight.

panels.shot: medium shot, low-angle, Lalitaditya on a temporary wooden viewing platform overlooking the open plain

dialogue.text: Around the 740s, Lalitaditya Muktapida turned from campaigns to creation. Here, near modern Paraspore, he chose a bare rise for a new royal seat: Parihasapura, City of Laughter.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Lalitaditya’s thoughtful face as he studies a palm-leaf plan

dialogue.text: Kalhana lists not one shrine but a whole complex: palace, Vishnu temples, a chaitya and a towering Buddha. This was urban planning, not just piety—a city to declare what Kashmir had become.

panels.shot: wide construction shot, bird’s-eye over coordinated building sites

dialogue.text: At Parihasapura, royal and sacred buildings rose together. The palace and the temples shared courtyards and sight-lines, binding king, gods and Buddha into one planned landscape.

panels.shot: low-angle shot along a colonnade of the emerging palace

dialogue.text: Kalhana calls the royal residence at Parihasapura a palace that invited laughter—parihasa—by its delight. The name itself tied joy to power, as if the capital should smile in stone.

panels.shot: wide shot of temple plinths being laid out with geometric precision

dialogue.text: To one side he ordered grand Vishnu temples; to another, a Buddhist chaitya. Their positions were no accident. The city’s plan itself showed a ruler who placed different paths side by side.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle on framework of enormous Buddha statue under construction

dialogue.text: Most striking, Kalhana describes a colossal Buddha image, sheathed in shining copper. Its exact height is lost in royal exaggeration, but its scale and metallic gleam marked a new ambition.

panels.shot: close-up on copper plates and gilding tools laid out on mats

dialogue.text: Kalhana’s verses revel in gold, silver and copper. The exact quantities are courtly flourish, yet they point to real monumental wealth—metal used not just as ornament but as architectural skin.

panels.shot: wide ceremonial shot of the completed core complex

dialogue.text: When the core was ready, the city looked like a stone mandala: king’s court at the center, Vaishnava shrines and Buddhist sanctuaries radiating out. Parihasapura announced a Karkota world in balance.

panels.shot: medium shot on a balcony overlooking the complex at dusk

dialogue.text: From his balcony the king saw not just buildings, but a message: that Kashmir’s ruler could sit amid many devotions, that laughter, light and learning belonged inside the frame of royal power.

panels.shot: slow push-in on mixed gathering in the main court

dialogue.text: Parihasapura functioned as more than a showpiece. Kalhana’s careful temple list hints at ongoing ritual and patronage, making the city a lived center of Karkota administration and religion.

panels.shot: contrast panel, modern-era wide shot of scattered stone bases at Paraspore

dialogue.text: By Stein’s visit in 1892, much had already gone. Stones from Parihasapura’s platforms edged new roads; pillars lay fallen in fields. The planned city survived only as ruins and a memory in verse.

panels.shot: close-up on an archaeologist’s hand tracing a carved stone at the site

dialogue.text: Stein matched Kalhana’s description to Paraspore’s ruins, sketching plans where stratigraphy is still thin. Without full excavation, scholars like Goetz read the stones and texts together for clues.

panels.shot: illustrative montage of art influences radiating outward on a map

dialogue.text: Art historians see in Parihasapura’s complex signs of wider influence—a Kashmiri way of arranging palace and shrines that may have echoed in Himalayan and north Indian building in later centuries.

panels.shot: evocative fade between Lalitaditya’s ancient silhouette and the present-day ruins

dialogue.text: Parihasapura no longer laughs in stone. Yet through Kalhana’s careful verses and the scattered remains, Lalitaditya’s experiment in shaping a capital as a statement of identity still speaks to us.
